How would a rolling shutter cause the pictured effect?

https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/49/Rolling_shutter_SMIL.svg
Because the flash from the lightning only lasts long enough that small part of the frame is being exposed while the sky is lit by the flash, giving the appearance of a column of light.

Digital camera sensors sweep left to right collecting light data, they don't collect it all at once. So each column of pixels technically represents a slightly different moment in time. If you are recording something that doesn't last very long, like lightning, then the event will only change the color of some of the columns of pixels like you see in this image.
Shitty digital cameras do that (like phones). Proper digital cameras have a real shutter and don't do that.

Not true. Higher end DSLRs have a feature called high speed shutter sync that mitigates this effect when it would be otherwise caused by the flash of a digital strobe, but it requires firing the strobe once for each section of the sensor that's exposed at the time.

It is true, actually. CCD sensors capture the entire frame at once, only CMOS has the rolling shutter. This doesn't look like a rolling shutter effect to me, personally. It's probably just a force field or something.

All CMOS sensors can have the effect, but DSLRs generally have a much faster readout speed than phones. It's much more rare to see the effect with a DSLR.
